summary: Describes the Remote Framebuffer protocol used by VNC for viewing and controlling the graphical interface of another computer. Because it works at the framebuffer level it applies to any windowing system. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Like watching someone else's screen through a window and also using their mouse and keyboard from far away.

subtitle: Viewing and controlling a remote desktop over the network.

tldr.problem: System administrators and remote users need to see and control the graphical interface of a computer on another network. Existing solutions are often tied to a specific windowing system (X11, Windows, etc.) or require complex protocol translation.
tldr.mechanism: RFB (Remote Framebuffer) sends pixel rectangles from the server's framebuffer to the client on demand. The client requests updates, sets the pixel format and encoding, and sends keyboard and pointer events. The server negotiates protocol version and security (password or none), then sends rectangles of pixel data in various encodings (Raw, CopyRect, Hextile, TRLE, ZRLE).
tldr.outcome: Users can access their applications from anywhere with network connectivity, see the exact same interface from multiple locations, and the interface state is preserved between sessions. RFB is the protocol used by VNC (Virtual Network Computing).

today: RFC 6143 documents RFB as it has been implemented in VNC and other remote desktop tools. It is informational and reflects historical practice going back a decade. It has not been obsoleted and remains the specification for RFB implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFB (Remote Framebuffer) is a protocol for remote graphical access that works by sending pixel data. Because it operates at the framebuffer level—below the windowing system—it works on any platform: X11, Windows, Macintosh, and others. RFB is used by VNC (Virtual Network Computing). The protocol makes very few demands on the client, so clients can run on simple hardware. It is also stateless: a client can disconnect and reconnect to the same server, and the interface will be unchanged; a different client can connect and see the same desktop.
sections.plainLanguage: RFB lets you see any computer's screen on another computer, even if they use different operating systems.

sections.title: Connection and Handshake
sections.content: An RFB server listens on TCP port 5900 (or port 5900+N for server N). Some servers also provide an HTTP server on port 5800 with a Java applet for browser-based access. The client contacts the server, which sends a ProtocolVersion message as a 12-byte ASCII string: RFB xxx.yyy\n (e.g., RFB 003.008\n). The client replies with its chosen version, which must not be higher than the server's. Then the server lists its supported security types (None or VNC Authentication). The client selects one; if VNC Authentication is chosen, the server sends a 16-byte challenge which the client encrypts with DES using the user's password (truncated to 8 chars) as the key, then sends the 16-byte response. Finally, the server sends a SecurityResult (0 for OK, 1 for failed).
sections.plainLanguage: First, the two computers shake hands: the server says 'I speak version 3.8', the client says 'OK, so do I', then they agree on whether to ask for a password.

sections.title: Initialization and Pixel Format
sections.content: After security is established, the client sends a ClientInit message with a shared-flag (0 to have exclusive access, 1 to share the desktop). The server responds with a ServerInit message containing the framebuffer width and height in pixels, the server's natural pixel format, and the desktop name. The client negotiates pixel format with SetPixelFormat: specifying bits-per-pixel (8, 16, or 32), depth, byte order (big-endian or little-endian), and for true color, the red/green/blue maximum values and shift amounts to extract color components from a pixel value. The client also sends SetEncodings to list the encodings it prefers (in priority order), such as ZRLE, TRLE, Hextile, or Raw, plus pseudo-encodings that declare support for extensions (Cursor or DesktopSize).
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server agree on how to draw: what colors to use, how big the screen is, and whether to squeeze the pixel data to save bandwidth.

sections.title: Display Updates
sections.content: The core of the RFB display protocol is the FramebufferUpdate, a server-to-client message containing a sequence of rectangles. The client drives all updates by sending FramebufferUpdateRequest messages with the region of interest (x, y, width, height) and an incremental flag: 0 requests the full contents of that area, 1 requests only changes. The server responds at its own pace with a FramebufferUpdate containing one or more rectangles that have changed. Each rectangle header specifies its position, size, and encoding type. The pixel data follows, encoded as specified. The six defined encodings are: Raw (uncompressed pixels), CopyRect (copy from elsewhere on the screen, for moves and scrolls), RRE (rise-and-run-length, obsolete), Hextile (16x16 tiles with RRE subrectangles, obsolete), TRLE (tiled run-length with palettization), and ZRLE (compressed tiles). Modern implementations prefer ZRLE, TRLE and CopyRect for best compression.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks the server 'show me what changed in this rectangle', and the server sends back the new picture. To save bandwidth, the server squeezes the picture using clever compression.

sections.title: Input Events and Protocol Extensions
sections.content: The client sends KeyEvent messages (key symbol from the X Window System, plus a down flag) and PointerEvent messages (x and y position, plus a button mask for up to 8 buttons). The client also sends ClientCutText to share clipboard text. The server can send Bell to make a sound and ServerCutText for clipboard sharing. The RFB protocol has evolved through versions 3.3, 3.7, and 3.8. New encodings can be added by clients requesting them in SetEncodings; servers that don't support a new encoding simply ignore it. Pseudo-encodings (negative numbers) let a client declare support for extensions without requiring a version bump (e.g., Cursor pseudo-encoding -239 for remote cursor, DesktopSize pseudo-encoding -223 for dynamic resize). New security types can also be added. Version numbers 3.9 and higher should not be used to maintain backward compatibility; future versions will use 4.x.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends keystrokes and mouse movements, and the server sends back sounds and clipboard text. New features are added without breaking old programs.
